lead: Ask three people how an order becomes an invoice and you hear three different processes, all prettier than the real one. The map that works for redesign comes from following real cases: the normal path, the detours, who decides what, and how long each thing takes. In this lesson you build that map on one page.
objetivo: map the normal path, the detours, the decisions, and today's measurements of a process, from an interview and from cases you followed.

aprende.t: The six blocks of a map that works for redesign
Interview the owner and follow five cases
Separate rule-based decisions from judgment-based decisions
Measure volume, people-minutes, rework, and waiting

hero_alt: In the warehouse aisle, the sales manager holds a tablet and watches a stock clerk pack jugs of detergent into a box.

secoes.sub: Scroll the page: each block lights up its part of the map. It is the same map for Horizonte and for your process.

nos.detalhe: What starts the process, through which channel, and from whom. "Customer sends the order on WhatsApp" is a trigger. "Sales" is not. If you can't name the trigger, you don't know where to start counting time.
The steps in the order they happen when nothing goes wrong, each one with who does it and in which system. It's the tagging sheet from lesson 1, now with wait time and people-minutes on each line.

Where the path splits. For each decision, the test: would two well-trained people, with the same information, always give the same answer? If yes, it's a rule and can become a system. If not, it's judgment and stays with a person.

The paths a case takes when something is missing or goes wrong: where it leaves the normal path, where it returns, and how often this happens. Rework lives in the detours, and it's where an agent that only copies the normal path gets lost the most.

Volume per week, people-minutes per case, time from trigger to completion, rework and the longest wait. Each number says where it came from: counted in a system, observed in the cases or stated by someone (hypothesis).

What comes out of the process, for whom, and the criterion that says it's finished. "Invoice issued and sent to the customer" is a completion. Without it, the process has no end, and cycle time can't be measured.

rolagem_fim.texto: Trigger, normal path, decisions, detours, measures and completion, on one page. It's the raw material for the redesign in lesson 4 and the baseline in lesson 6.

secoes.sub: Four steps, in one week. The Horizonte data is fictional, for study.

texto: The process owner is the person who answers for the result, not the one who does the most steps. Ask about the trigger, the completion, the decisions and the detours they know. Use the script alongside.
The interview gives you the process as the owner thinks it is. Write everything down, but don't draw it yet: following the cases will correct a good part of it.

exemplo.texto: Patrícia answers for the order all the way to the invoice. In the interview, she described 9 steps. The cases we followed showed 13.

texto: Pick five real cases and follow each one from start to finish: time of each step, people-minutes, where it detoured. Prefer cases that differ from each other: a common one, one with a decision, one that went wrong.
Five cases are exploration, not a sample. They're for drawing the map and finding where to measure, not for stating an average to Carlos.

exemplo.texto: From 10/15 to 10/17, Patrícia followed five orders: a normal one, one with a discount request, one from a customer without a CNPJ, one with a product shortage and one above R$ 5 thousand. The numbers are in the "The five cases" tab.

texto: Mark each point where the path splits. Write the decision's question and apply the test: would two trained people answer the same? A rule can become a system; judgment stays with someone, by name.
For each detour, note where it starts, where the case returns and what gets lost along the way: time, rework, customer waiting.

exemplo.texto: "Does the customer have a complete registration?" is a rule, but today it's only asked at invoicing, after picking. Case P3 came back from finance and took 75 hours to get to the invoice.

passos.sub: with the source of each number
texto: Four measures: volume per week, people-minutes per case, time from trigger to completion and rework. Add the longest wait: almost always, process time is queue, not work.

Every number carries its source: counted in a system, observed in the cases, or declared. Declared numbers go in as a hypothesis until they are counted; what's observed in five cases is a clue, and only becomes a baseline after weeks of counting (lesson 6).

exemplo.texto: 168 orders in the week of 10/13 (dashboard). Median of 21 minutes of people time and 30 hours until the invoice in the five cases. Rework: "about 15 a week come back," says finance (hypothesis).

secoes.titulo: Templates to copy: the map and the script
secoes.sub: The one-page map is the central template of the course. The script and the case sheet feed the map. The tabs show Horizonte.

abas.html:
Order via WhatsApp → invoice · v1.0 · owner: Patrícia · Horizonte, fictional study company

Trigger: customer sends the order via WhatsApp. Completion: invoice issued and sent to the customer in the conversation.

Normal path (13 steps): reply → enter in the app → copy to the spreadsheet → check the price of every item → approve above R$ 5 thousand → print and take to the warehouse → check availability in the ERP → pick → notify Juliana → email to finance → retype in the ERP → check the customer record and issue the invoice → send the invoice.

Decisions: discount within policy? (rule) · above R$ 5 thousand? (rule) · discount between 5% and 10%: give it or not? (Patrícia's judgment) · customer with a complete record? (rule, today only at step 12) · product out of stock: deliver partially or wait? (judgment, with the customer).

Detours: D1 incomplete record: finance sends it back to customer service after picking ("about 15 a week," declared = hypothesis). D2 product out of stock: partial order, Juliana calls the customer (1 in 5 cases, observed).

Measures: 168 orders in the week of 10/13 (counted, dashboard) · 21 min of people time per order (median, 5 cases) · 30 h until the invoice (median, 5 cases) · longest wait: finance invoices the next morning, and the warehouse receives the papers in two batches (10 am and 3 pm).

Followed from 10/15 to 10/17/2026 · fictional · exploration, not a sample

CasePathPeople min.Until invoiceSent back?
P1 Bakery, R$ 1,240normal1622 hno
P2 Supermarket, R$ 4,320, asks for 8%discount decision2126 hno
P3 New customer without CNPJ, R$ 2,800D13875 hyes
P4 Restaurant, out of disinfectantD22749 hno
P5 Clinic, R$ 6,150approval above R$ 5 thousand1930 hno

Medians: 21 minutes of people time; 30 hours until the invoice. In every case, less than 40 minutes was work; the rest was waiting.

• A map the way the owner told it. If the map has fewer steps than the cases showed, you drew the interview.
  • Only the happy path. Without at least two detours, the map hides where the rework is.
  • An average of five cases sold as truth. Five cases show where to measure; the number for deciding comes from lesson 6.
  • A number with no origin. "About 15 a week" is declared: it enters as a hypothesis.
  • Personal data on the sheet. Use a code for the case, not the customer's name and phone.

secoes.sub: The Horizonte map with the five cases ready; yours with cases you follow yourself.
secoes.fonte: Lab pieces: WhatsApp agent and dashboard (fictional study company).

exercicios.texto: Use the 13 steps from lesson 1 and the "The five cases" tab to fill in the one-page map of the "order via WhatsApp → invoicing" process. Calculate the medians yourself. Run the gaps prompt and answer what it raises.
exercicios.pronto: the map has a trigger and a completion, the 13 steps with who and system, at least 4 decisions marked as rule or judgment, the 2 detours with where they go back to, today's measures (volume, median minutes, median time, rework) each with its origin, and the longest wait identified.

exercicios.texto: For the process you chose in lesson 2: interview the owner with the script and follow five cases with the sheet, without changing anything in the process. Then build the one-page map.
exercicios.pronto: the interview is noted with a date, the 5 case sheets are filled in, and the map has a trigger, completion, normal path, at least 2 detours, the decisions marked, and the 4 measures with origin.

secoes.sub: 5 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: The owner described 9 steps; the cases followed showed 13. Which map counts?
opcoes: The owner's, because they answer for the result and know the exceptions
The owner's, completed with the steps the team finds useful
The cases': the map shows what happens, not what people remember
perguntas.explica: The interview shows the process as the owner thinks it is. The 4 steps nobody remembered to count (copying, printing, notifying) are exactly the candidates to go in the redesign; completing the owner's map with opinion repeats the mistake.

perguntas.p: "Does the customer have a complete record?" Two trained people, with the same record open, would answer the same. What is it?
opcoes: Judgment: it depends on who knows the customer and their history
Rule: it can become a system check, right when the order is entered
Judgment: an incomplete record is sometimes accepted by finance
perguntas.explica: Same information, same answer: it's a rule. Knowing the customer's history doesn't change whether the CNPJ is in the record or not. Horizonte's problem isn't who answers, it's where: the question only shows up at invoicing, after picking.

perguntas.p: In the five cases, the median was 21 minutes of people time and 30 hours until the invoice. What does that suggest?
opcoes: That almost all the time is waiting between steps, not work
That the work in each step is slow and needs more people
That only an agent working at night would fix the total time
perguntas.explica: 21 minutes of work in 30 hours: the time is in the queues (warehouse batches, invoicing the next day). Speeding up the work in each step barely changes the total; removing waits and handoffs does.

perguntas.p: Finance says "about 15 orders a week come back." How does it go on the map?
opcoes: As 15 per week, measured, because finance sees all the orders
It stays off the map until someone counts it, so it doesn't contaminate the measurement
As a hypothesis declared by finance, to be counted later
perguntas.explica: Declared counts as a clue and goes in with its source marked. Throwing it out loses the clue; treating it as measured misleads whoever decides. Counting comes in lesson 6.

perguntas.p: Why follow only five cases, and not a hundred?
opcoes: Because five well-chosen cases already give the process average
To draw the map and find where to measure; the measurement that decides comes later
Because following more cases would change the process during the observation
perguntas.explica: Five cases are exploration: they show hidden steps, detours, and waits, but they don't give a reliable average. To say how long the process takes, and to compare before and after, you need weeks of counted data (lesson 6).

itens.texto: Trigger, normal path, decisions, detours, measurements, conclusion.
An interview gives you the hypothesis; five followed cases correct the map.
Same information, same answer: rule. Otherwise, it stays with a person.
Counted, observed, or declared. The time is almost always in the waiting.
